title: Buchanan Associate Professor of Business Administration
bio: We study why microfinance borrowers who could benefit from larger, more flexible loans often fail to “graduate” out of standard microcredit. While graduation loans have been shown to improve livelihoods, we show that a key barrier lies inside lending organizations themselves. In many microfinance institutions, loan officers are compensated based on the size and repayment performance of their microloan portfolios. When a strong borrower graduates to a larger loan managed by a different team, the original loan officer effectively loses compensation. This creates a hidden penalty for graduation and an incentive to withhold referrals—even when graduation is in the borrower’s and the institution’s best interest. Working with one of Chile’s largest microfinance institutions, we implement a large-scale field experiment that changes loan officer compensation to reduce and then partially reverse this penalty. When incentives are realigned, loan officers refer significantly more borrowers for graduation. Importantly, borrowers referred after the compensation change perform substantially better: they repay graduation loans at higher rates and experience significantly greater business growth than borrowers referred under the original incentive scheme. This indicates that loan officers were not only withholding referrals, but disproportionately withholding their most qualified borrowers. Using global data and a new survey of microfinance institutions, we show that these incentive structures are common: nearly half of institutions with internal graduation programs employ compensation practices similar to those we study. Our findings highlight how misaligned internal incentives can limit the impact of well-designed financial products, even in mission-driven organizations. More broadly, our results apply to any organization that relies on internal referrals, demonstrating how thoughtful incentive design can unlock growth, improve outcomes, and better align organizational behavior with strategic goals.
